title: Beetles o’er his base
html_source:
Quote from Hamlet, spoken by Horatio when warning Hamlet not to follow his father’s ghost in case it tricks him to falling to his doom. ‘Beetle’ is used in the uncommon sense of ‘to overhang’ (collinsdictionary.com)

Stephen has left Deasy in the school in Dalkey to deliver his letter to the editor of The homestead or to meet Mulligan in The Ship. A virgin reader won’t know which he chooses. The veteran reader (terminology coined by Margot Norris) knows there is a great stand off in the national library about Hamlet in a couple of hours. Joyce sets us a little hint as to what happens here. One reference to what Stephen intends to do amidst his wild philosophical musings on the strand indicates his displaced frame of mind that morning.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Missing that:
(1) Hamlet is used not merely as an external text which the characters are intrigued with and frequently reference but as a very metaphor for the action, the substance of the novel (You will find Haines himself draws a parallel between the Martello tower and the cliffs of Elsinore early on.)
(2) I agree with the last sentence; however, to continue the reading from this frame I have suggested, this should be considered as an explicit link between Hamlet and Stephen, the ghost of Hamlet’s father and Stephen’s dead mother who appears always smelling of rosewater and wetted ashes.
(3) This sentence and several that follow it, suggest the anxiety of walking blindly (I mean literally, since Stephen does shut his eyes). Readers may want to consider that Joyce was blind– therefore, the modality of sight would be a significant meditation.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Spanish translate: Si yo cayera sobre una escollera que se desborda sobre su base, ¡si me cayera a través del nebeneinander ineluctablemente! (Subirat)

But…
I read about this sentences and I don’t understand why to skip the ‘coleoptero’. Several species of dung beetle, especially the “sacred scarab” Scarabaeus sacer, were revered by the ancient Egyptians. The scarab was linked to Khepri, the god of the rising sun, from the supposed resemblance of the dung ball rolled by the beetle to the rolling of the sun by the god.[79] Plutarch wrote:
The race of beetles has no female, but all the males eject their sperm into a round pellet of material which they roll up by pushing it from the opposite side, just as the sun seems to turn the heavens in the direction opposite to its own course, which is from west to east.

(wikipedia)
